Single-image raindrop removal models struggle to extract large-scale raindrop features, limiting accuracy in complex real-world scenes. This paper proposes a high-order recursive network (HORNet) comprising three components. First, a dual-scale attention residual module combines channel attention (SE), grouped convolution, and residual branches to capture large-scale raindrop features; grouped convolution with 3×3 and 5×5 kernels yields the best configuration. Second, a high-order recursive feature transfer mechanism couples local recursion R1 (parameter reuse across dual-scale modules) and global recursion R2 (multi-stage inference guided by previous stage outputs). Third, a dual-scale residual gated recurrent unit (GRU) introduces feedback across recursive stages via modified input gates and hidden-state convolutions. Training uses a joint SSIM and MAE loss (λ=0.6), Adam optimizer, 100×100 crops, batch size 2, 24 epochs, and initial learning rate 0.001 decayed by 1/5 at epochs 6, 12, and 18 on PyTorch 1.6 with an NVIDIA 2080Ti. On benchmark Test_A and Test_B, the model achieves PSNR/SSIM of 31.41 dB/0.934 and 26.17 dB/0.824, respectively, outperforming ten representative deep models including ATT-GAN, TransWeather, D-DAM, and MANAS by at least 1.29 dB and 1.25 dB PSNR on the two test sets.

The paper targets the limited capacity of single-image raindrop removal networks to model large, overlapping raindrops, which degrades accuracy in complex scenes. The proposed high-order recursive network replaces standard convolution stacks with a dual-scale attention residual module using grouped 3×3/5×5 kernels, and adds a two-level recursion scheme (local R1, global R2) plus a dual-scale residual GRU for inter-stage feedback. On public benchmarks, the model reaches 31.41 dB PSNR / 0.934 SSIM (Test_A) and 26.17 dB / 0.824 (Test_B), beating ten representative deep models by at least 1.25–1.29 dB PSNR.

The design trades additional recursive computation for accuracy: excessive recursion (e.g., R1=1, R2=3) collapses performance to 17.94 dB PSNR due to feature redundancy and overfitting, while the optimal R1=2, R2=2 balances local feature extraction and global refinement. Training is lightweight (100×100 crops, batch size 2, 24 epochs, single NVIDIA 2080Ti), suggesting practical deployability for camera or windshield vision pipelines, though real-world generalization beyond the two benchmark test sets remains to be validated.
## Dual-Scale Attention Residual Module with Grouped Convolution

The dual-scale attention residual module integrates a squeeze-and-excitation (SE) channel attention mechanism, grouped convolution, and a standard residual branch. Input features first pass through the SE block to reweight channel responses, then are split into two groups along the channel dimension (group count = 2). Each group is processed by grouped convolution with different kernel sizes—3×3 and 5×5—to capture edge and contour structures of large-scale raindrops. Rather than generating all feature maps via grouped convolution, part of the grouped-convolution output is concatenated with the original feature map, preserving feature diversity while reducing computation and memory. Input and output channel dimensions are kept identical across the module and each branch, avoiding extra convolution operations.

Ablation on module structure (Table 1) shows standard convolution (3,3) yields 25.11 dB PSNR / 0.883 SSIM on Test_A and 22.89 dB / 0.785 on Test_B; standard convolution (3,5) gives 25.33 dB / 0.883 and 22.93 dB / 0.783. Single-scale grouped convolution (1,1) already improves Test_A PSNR to 26.51 dB (+1.2 dB over standard 3,5), confirming the benefit of grouped convolution. Single-scale grouped convolution (3,3) and (5,5) raise Test_A PSNR to 31.11 dB and 31.16 dB, with SSIM 0.931–0.932. The dual-scale grouped convolution (3,5) achieves the best results: 31.41 dB / 0.934 on Test_A and 26.17 dB / 0.824 on Test_B, providing multi-scale receptive fields.
**Table (Dual-Scale Attention Residual Module with Grouped Convolution)**
## High-Order Recursive Feature Transfer and Dual-Scale Residual GRU Validation

The high-order recursive feature transfer mechanism combines local recursion R1 (parameter reuse across a set of dual-scale attention residual modules) and global recursion R2 (multi-stage inference where the current stage's restored image guides the next stage). Table 2 reports hyperparameter sweeps: without recursion (R1=1, R2=1), PSNR is only 25.09 dB / 0.815 on Test_A and 22.39 dB / 0.726 on Test_B. Increasing global recursion alone (R1=1, R2=2 or 3) degrades performance to 21.37 dB / 0.642 and 17.94 dB / 0.488, attributed to poor local feature extraction being amplified. Setting R1=2 lifts Test_A PSNR to 30.61 dB / 0.928; the optimal combination R1=2, R2=2 reaches 31.41 dB / 0.934 and 26.17 dB / 0.824. Further increases (R1=3 or R2=3) cause slight declines due to feature redundancy and overfitting.

The dual-scale residual gated recurrent unit (GRU) modifies the input gate and hidden-state convolution to enable feedback across recursive stages. Table 3 compares variants: without GRU, PSNR is 30.74 dB / 0.927 (Test_A) and 25.72 dB / 0.813 (Test_B); a local-recursion-only GRU gives 31.09 dB / 0.932 and 25.93 dB / 0.822; a global-recursion-only GRU gives 30.86 dB / 0.930 and 25.79 dB / 0.819; the full dual-scale residual GRU achieves 31.41 dB / 0.934 and 26.17 dB / 0.824, i.e., +0.67 dB and +0.45 dB over the no-GRU model. Training uses a joint loss L = λ(1−SSIM) + (1−λ)MAE with λ=0.6, Adam optimizer, 100×100 crops, batch size 2, 24 epochs, and initial learning rate 0.001 decayed by 1/5 at epochs 6, 12, and 18.
**Table (High-Order Recursive Feature Transfer and Dual-Scale Residual GRU Validation)**
## Recursion Depth Sensitivity and Benchmark Generalization Boundaries
- Excessive global recursion without sufficient local recursion (R1=1, R2=3) collapses PSNR to 17.94 dB on Test_A and 17.42 dB on Test_B, indicating strong sensitivity to the R1/R2 balance.
- Increasing recursion beyond R1=2, R2=2 causes feature redundancy and overfitting, reducing test-set generalization and consuming additional computation.
- Evaluation is limited to two public benchmark test sets (Test_A sparse, Test_B complex); no real-world deployment or cross-dataset generalization results are reported.
- Training uses 100×100 crops, batch size 2, and a single NVIDIA 2080Ti, with no reported inference latency or parameter count for deployment planning.",1179,"

## Speech Modulation Spectrum Priors and Multi-Scale Temporal Convolutions

Conventional neural decoders for non-invasive electroencephalogram (EEG) signals rely on uniform temporal filters that fail to capture the multi-tiered temporal structure intrinsic to human language processing. Neurological research indicates that speech perception and internal speech production selectively track acoustic envelopes modulated below 16 Hz. Specifically, modulation frequencies around 16 Hz align with phoneme-level transitions, 8 Hz corresponds to sub-syllabic stress patterns, 4 Hz synchronizes with syllabic rhythms, and frequencies below 2 Hz convey phrase-level prosody.

Rather than assigning arbitrary temporal receptive fields, the model instantiates three parallel 1D depthwise temporal convolution branches with kernel durations of 125 ms (size 32), 250 ms (size 64), and 500 ms (size 128). An unconv-olved residual branch retains ultra-slow prosodic envelopes below 2 Hz, ensuring complete hierarchical coverage.
- Phoneme branch: 125 ms temporal receptive field targeting 16 Hz modulation frequencies.
- Sub-syllable branch: 250 ms temporal receptive field capturing 8 Hz stress transitions.
- Syllable branch: 500 ms temporal receptive field matching 4 Hz linguistic pacing.
- Residual branch: Direct envelope passthrough preserving sub-2 Hz phrasal structures.

Cortical activation patterns during silent speech imagery vary dynamically across linguistic granularities. To prevent sub-optimal uniform spatial pooling, KMST-Former introduces scale-specific Efficient Channel Attention (ECA) directly onto each temporal processing path. After temporal global average pooling summarizes channel-wise energy distributions, a lightweight adaptive 1D convolution dynamically computes interaction weights across neighboring electrodes without dimensionality reduction, steering network focus toward phoneme- or syllable-sensitive scalp topographies.

Following channel recalibration, features across all four branches are concatenated into an expanded channel dimension of 4C. To prevent disruptive cross-scale interference, a two-stage fusion mechanism organizes feature integration. Stage one applies a grouped 1D convolution with four groups to compress and align intra-scale representations independently. Stage two uses standard 1D convolutions to execute comprehensive cross-scale and cross-channel blending, projecting the unified embeddings into token vectors for Transformer sequence encoding.
- Lightweight channel attention: Avoids fully connected bottlenecks by learning local cross-channel interactions via 1D convolutions.
- Stage one grouping: Isolates intra-scale compression to prevent premature multi-frequency feature blurring.
- Stage two projection: Executes full cross-scale synthesis into fixed token dimensions before sequence modeling.

## Empirical Benchmark Performance Across Within-Subject and Mixed-Subject Tasks

Systematic validation was executed on the BCI2020 silent speech imagery benchmark, which comprises 15 healthy human subjects performing 5-class imagined vocabulary prompts (Hello, Help me, Stop, Thank you, Yes) with 300 training, 50 validation, and 50 test trials per subject. While KMST-Former advances structured neural decoding for speech brain-computer interfaces, several experimental boundaries define its operational scope.

- The experimental protocol evaluates isolated 5-class discrete word imagery (Hello, Help me, Stop, Thank you, Yes) rather than unconstrained continuous speech or open-vocabulary sentences.

## Multipinhole PPDF Classification and Gaussian Parameterization

In stationary multi-pinhole large-animal SPECT systems, the system transfer matrix maps emission probabilities from discrete image voxels to detector pixels. Exhaustive empirical calibration over 223,260 positions is prohibitive given the physical decay of 99mTc and mechanical stage latency. Because the projection probability density function (PPDF) varies smoothly across spatial coordinates along the detector plane, the matrix elements exhibit continuous geometric structure. Ray distribution geometry across the detector ring determines three distinct response states: zero-photon exposure, single-pinhole irradiation, or overlapping multi-pinhole irradiation.

An automated classification algorithm stratifies PPDF responses across the detector domain. Non-illuminated pixels, accounting for 56.96% of the volume, are directly set to zero to eliminate unnecessary numerical optimization. Single-pinhole contributions, representing 34.43% of cases, are parameterized as an asymmetric two-dimensional Gaussian profile with 6 independent coefficients. Multi-pinhole overlapping signals, constituting 8.61%, are modeled as a linear combination of two 2D Gaussian functions encompassing 12 parameters. Initialized by the classification algorithm, parameters are optimized using the Levenberg-Marquardt least-squares solver.
- Automated triage segregates pixels into zero (56.96%), single-signal (34.43%), and multi-signal (8.61%) distributions.

## Multi-Scale Wavelet Decomposition and Hierarchical Autoencoder Reconstruction Architecture

In modern industrial Internet of Things deployments, real-time telemetry gathered across turbomachinery, chemical reactors, and nuclear power auxiliary equipment drives condition-based maintenance, remaining useful life estimation, and incipient failure detection. Nevertheless, operational telemetry continuously suffers from missing values induced by harsh environmental interference, transient bus drops, and intermittent sensor failures. Traditional imputation strategies, such as k-nearest neighbors, expectation-maximization, and single-scale deep autoencoders, optimize global profile reconstruction. In doing so, they attenuate high-frequency transients and local vibrational perturbations. These omitted subtle signals, however, represent the precise physical indicators necessary to isolate developing component malfunctions.

To resolve this structural deficiency, the wavelet transform-based missing value imputation (WTMI) framework disassembles raw multivariate sequences into multi-resolution subbands using discrete wavelet transforms. Low-frequency approximation components retain macro-level operational trends, whereas high-frequency detail subbands isolate localized structural oscillations. Individual subbands are routed into independent deep autoencoders to reconstruct uncorrupted scale representations. The completed multi-channel series is subsequently assembled via inverse discrete wavelet transformation. By partitioning feature recovery across isolated spectral tiers, WTMI prevents dominant low-frequency trends from overwhelming critical diagnostic details.
- Decomposes raw sensor matrices into decoupled approximation and detail coefficient tensors across arbitrary scale depths.
- Prevents oversmoothing of localized transient spikes by isolating high-frequency subbands within targeted autoencoder pipelines.
- Initializes unobserved values with linear interpolation prior to decomposition to reduce boundary wave distortion.

## Stacked Cross-Scale Recurrent Neural Feature Fusion and Consistency Constraints

While independent subband reconstruction improves local feature recovery, treating decomposition layers in isolation ignores the hierarchical correlation between broad operating shifts and localized physical responses. Furthermore, selecting an optimal decomposition depth often demands extensive empirical tuning. The multi-scale missing value imputation (MSMI) architecture addresses these hurdles by implementing a top-down stacked gated recurrent unit (GRU) network inspired by deep stacking network topologies. Rather than restricting decomposition depth, MSMI decomposes signals across a generous scale horizon, feeding all approximation and detail coefficient matrices into the model simultaneously.

In the MSMI formulation, the hidden representation derived from the coarsest scale encoder is mapped through a learnable projection matrix and bilinear upsampling operator to initialize the hidden state of the adjacent finer-scale GRU encoder. Multi-scale bottleneck representations are concatenated, compressed into a channel descriptor via average pooling, and reweighted through sigmoid activation to produce an integrated fusion vector. This multi-scale representation directly steers parallel GRU decoders across each frequency tier. To enforce strict mathematical compatibility between adjacent tiers, a cross-scale consistency loss penalizes deviations between reconstructed detail coefficients and the discrete wavelet transform of inverse-reconstructed coarser coefficients.
- Establishes a top-down recurrence hierarchy where coarse-scale semantic states guide fine-scale high-frequency detail synthesis.
- Applies a squeeze-and-excitation style channel attention mechanism across bottleneck vectors to dynamically weight scale contributions.
- Incorporates an explicit wavelet reconstruction penalty ensuring reconstructed subbands obey inverse mathematical identities.

- Maintains narrow error residual distributions, effectively preventing catastrophic outlier imputations during prolonged sensor dropouts.
- Supplies highly discriminative reconstructed features that elevate downstream SVM classification accuracy across component, degradation, and weak fault categories.

- Balancing coefficient theta regulates the mutual objective between raw reconstruction fidelity and diagnostic classification; setting theta too high progressively degrades imputation accuracy.

Manual interpretation of dynamometer cards for beam pumping units is inefficient and cannot quantitatively track the slow evolution of liquid supply capacity in low-yield oil wells. Conventional data-driven models achieve high accuracy but lack physical interpretability and are difficult to deploy on edge hardware. This work proposes a physics-informed lightweight spatiotemporal visual perception model. Suspension-point displacement and load time series are rendered as normalized 200×100-pixel grayscale images, and a dedicated dataset, Low-YieldD (15,000 labeled cards, 8:1:1 split), is built via wave-equation simulation and iterative intelligent annotation. A cascaded temporal-forecasting/spatial-recognition architecture couples a dual-stream LSTM, which predicts future card morphology, with a lightweight CNN. A physics-informed spatial attention (PISA) mechanism encodes the fluid-pound delay as a differentiable Gaussian spatial mask, steering the CNN toward the unloading zone. The model uses 0.79 M parameters, 1.3% of standard AlexNet, yet reaches 99.1% liquid-supply-capacity recognition accuracy and a physical-plausibility score of 0.93, outperforming MobileNetV2, ShuffleNetV2, EfficientNet-Lite and SqueezeNet. On a Huawei Atlas 500 edge gateway over one month, response delay fell 87.5%, monthly ineffective pumping dropped 59.7%, and power consumption per ton of liquid decreased 22.0%.

The bottleneck addressed is the mismatch between accurate but opaque deep models and the compute, memory and power limits of oilfield edge gateways, compounded by the inability of static classifiers to track slow degradation of liquid supply. The paper resolves this by converting displacement-load signals into 200×100 grayscale cards, predicting future card morphology with a dual-stream LSTM, and constraining a 0.79 M-parameter CNN with a differentiable Gaussian mask derived from the fluid-pound delay mechanism. The trade-off is explicit: inference takes 8.3 ms, slower than SqueezeNet's 3.9 ms, in exchange for a physical-plausibility score of 0.93 versus 0.65 and accuracy of 99.1% versus 95.3%.

R&D relevance centers on the annotation pipeline and the deployment evidence. Iterative intelligent annotation, seeded with roughly 10% expert labels and expanded by uncertainty sampling, produced 15,000 cards whose simulated and measured normalized unloading-line lengths pass a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test (p>0.05, Cohen's d=0.065). A one-month run on a Huawei Atlas 500 gateway with quantization, cache retransmission and cloud-edge collaboration delivered 87.5% lower response delay and 22.0% lower energy per ton, indicating that physics-guided attention can substitute for parameter count in narrow industrial vision tasks.
## Dual-Stream LSTM Temporal Forecasting and PISA-Guided Lightweight CNN

The architecture is a cascade of temporal forecasting and spatial recognition. Displacement and load channels are preprocessed separately: displacement is cubic-spline interpolated and split at the maximum displacement point into upstroke and downstroke segments, while load is handled on its own branch. A dual-stream coupled LSTM models the evolution of card sequences and predicts the next five time steps (1T–5T), reproducing the gradual lengthening of the 'knife-handle' segment that signals declining supply. The recognition stage is a redesigned AlexNet: input 200×100×1 grayscale, first-layer kernels reduced from 64 11×11/stride 4 to 64 7×7/stride 2, subsequent layers at 128 3×3, 192 3×3, 192 3×3 and 128 3×3, and fully connected layers replaced by a 512-neuron hidden layer.

The physics-informed spatial attention module is inserted after the second convolutional layer. A 1×1 convolution compresses channels and maps features to an attention map; the fluid-pound delay is encoded as a differentiable Gaussian spatial mask that biases attention toward the unloading zone. Training uses 200 epochs, batch size 32, batch normalization and dropout at 0.5. The resulting model holds 0.79 M parameters, about 1.3% of standard AlexNet, and performs inference in 8.3 ms. Ablation shows accuracy of 92.7% for the base model, 95.3% with generic attention, and 99.1% with PISA, while the physical-plausibility score moves from 0.71 to 0.82 to 0.93 and gradient error on unloading-line length falls 70.7%.

column1: ## Low-YieldD Dataset Construction and Edge-Gateway Field Validation

Low-YieldD contains 15,000 labeled grayscale cards from 20 typical low-yield wells in a Changqing oilfield block, augmented by wave-equation simulation. Simulation parameters follow API Spec 11B and historical well statistics: pump depth 800–2,950 m, crude viscosity 5–200 mPa·s, mixture density 850–1,000 kg/m³, damping coefficient 0.5–5.0 s⁻¹, supply capacity 10–100%, and stroke rate 2–8 min⁻¹, sampled by Latin hypercube to extrapolate to the 10–30% edge regime. Labels are defined purely by visual morphology: the ratio of knife-handle pixel length to total contour length is divided into 10 grades at 10% intervals. Annotation is iterative, starting from about 10% expert-labeled seeds and expanding by uncertainty or representative sampling until validation accuracy meets threshold.

Validation statistics support simulation fidelity: the two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test on normalized unloading-line length gives p>0.05 with Cohen's d=0.065, and the auxiliary area feature differs by 2.2% (432.5 versus 441.8). Against lightweight baselines on the same split, the proposed model reaches 99.1% accuracy and 0.93 plausibility, versus 96.8%/0.71 for MobileNetV2 (3.50 M), 97.1%/0.68 for ShuffleNetV2 (2.85 M), 97.5%/0.73 for EfficientNet-Lite (4.52 M) and 95.3%/0.65 for SqueezeNet (1.25 M). A one-month deployment on a Huawei Atlas 500 gateway reports 99.1% accuracy, 30 min response delay, 25 monthly ineffective-pumping events, 33.3 kWh/t and 0.8 manual interventions per day, with predictive-maintenance efficiency at 92%.
**Table (Low-YieldD Dataset Construction and Edge-Gateway Field Validation)**
## Sensitivity Envelope, Annotation Dependence and Edge Deployment Constraints
- Accuracy stays above 98.5% under standard conditions but degrades at extreme viscosity and stroke-rate combinations, defining the current operating boundary.

- The model is sensitive to image quality and depends on pixel-level expert annotation of the unloading zone; three experts with over 10 years of experience labeled 200 test cards for the plausibility reference.
- The single-peak Gaussian prior has limited adaptability under extreme conditions; future work proposes physics-guided image augmentation, adversarial training and a PISA regularization term.
- Edge deployment requires model quantization, cache retransmission and cloud-edge collaboration on a Huawei Atlas 500 gateway to cope with unstable field networks and limited compute.",1198,"

STPredictor addresses the maritime industry's need for accurate and interpretable ship trajectory prediction by reformulating the task as a language modeling problem using LLMs. Unlike traditional predictors that rely on post-clustered trajectories and lack transparency, STPredictor encodes heterogeneous maritime scenarios as natural-language prompts and employs supervised fine-tuning with Chain-of-Thought reasoning. This approach yields substantial accuracy gains: RMSE reductions of 20–30% over the strongest baseline across all draught intervals, with particularly strong performance in deep-draught scenarios where ADE improves by over 40%. The model also achieves significantly lower angular errors, with AHE and FHE an order of magnitude smaller than baselines.

However, the superior accuracy comes at a computational cost: inference latency is 8.4 seconds per prediction, compared to milliseconds for conventional deep learning models. This trade-off between interpretability/accuracy and real-time performance is critical for practical deployment. The authors suggest future work on LLM compression techniques to achieve real-time performance. The method's reliance on AIS data and LLM fine-tuning may require substantial computational resources for training and deployment, but the open-source replication package (ETSD) facilitates further research. ## STPredictor Architecture: LLM-Based Trajectory Prediction with Chain-of-Thought

STPredictor reformulates ship trajectory prediction as a language modeling problem. Heterogeneous maritime scenarios, including geospatial coordinates, ship draught, and environmental context, are encoded as natural-language prompts. The core model is built upon LLaMA (Touvron et al., 2023) and fine-tuned with supervised learning to specialize for trajectory prediction. The inference pipeline integrates a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) process, where the model generates intermediate reasoning steps before outputting the predicted trajectory. This design enhances transparency and reliability, allowing the decision process to align with human instructions. The model outputs a sequence of future waypoints, and evaluation metrics include RMSE, ADE, FDE, AHE, and FHE, with a fixed prediction horizon of 6 steps.

The instruction-aligned approach incorporates maritime constraints and observed scenarios to enable interpretable and human-guided prediction. By leveraging the reasoning capabilities of LLMs, STPredictor captures complex interactions and contextual information that traditional sequence models may overlook. The fine-tuning process adapts the general-purpose LLM to the maritime domain, using the constructed AIS datasets. The CoT mechanism provides a window into the model's decision-making, which is crucial for safety-critical applications. The authors emphasize that this integration of semantic navigation intent and port-pose priors contributes to accurate course-over-ground (CoG) estimation, as evidenced by the low angular errors achieved.

## Experimental Validation on Geospatial and Draught-Based AIS Datasets

Two large-scale datasets were constructed from global AIS records: a geospatial-domain dataset and a draught-domain dataset. The geospatial dataset includes trajectories from specific water areas such as Zhoushan and SG, with varying numbers of waypoints (e.g., 286 and 115). The draught-based dataset categorizes trajectories by ship draught intervals: shallow (0–5 m), medium (10–25 m), and deep (>25 m). No AIS-based trajectory clustering was applied to avoid performance inflation from route-specific priors. The test set comprised 5,000 randomly selected frames, and each predictor was run five times to mitigate random variation. When the calculated symmetric divergence exceeds the calibrated threshold of 0.337, the pipeline confirms the presence of concurrent anomalies and directs both isolated signal channels to the multi-class recognizer. ## Multi-Information Voxel Space Decomposition and Geometry Pruning

Computing signed distance fields directly from raw triangular meshes via brute-force traversal requires evaluating distances from each query point to all n mesh facets, leading to an intractable per-point complexity of O(n). The proposed architecture partitions the axis-aligned bounding box into uniform voxels of edge length d, creating a dual-stage multi-information storage scheme. The initial space-partitioned voxel structure (Space) records triangle indices intersecting each discrete cubic box through bounding box overlap and separating axis theorem evaluations. This discretizes continuous surface boundaries into boundary voxels containing intersecting facets and empty non-boundary voxels.

A linear-time three-dimensional Euclidean distance transform computes an approximate signed distance field across the voxel grid, determining the minimum distance dt0 from each voxel center C to the nearest boundary voxel. Under established geometric bounds, any triangle capable of providing the absolute nearest surface distance to points within a given voxel must reside within a distance D < D0 + 3d, where D0 represents the distance to the closest known triangle. This establishes a spherical shell search zone constrained by dt(i,j,k) in [dt0, dt0 + 3/2 * 3d], which is approximated via a bounding hollow cube. Facets meeting this condition are assigned to a distance-partitioned voxel data structure termed SdfBox, decoupling all voxel-level subproblems and filtering out distant geometry so that only a small subset m of triangles is retained.

Finally, parameter updates for primary recommendation prediction task were performed through a cross-entropy loss function, and the multi-level contrastive learning tasks were used to assist in parameter updates of recommendation prediction tasks at embedding layer, node layer, and sequential layer; specifically, on the embedding layer and node layer for better item representations in recommendation prediction tasks, while on the sequential layer for better user representations in recommendation prediction tasks. The MLGCL-SR framework introduces a hierarchical contrastive learning architecture that structures user interaction sequences into item transition graphs and processes them with an optimized Bidirectional Gated Graph Neural Network (BI-GGNN). Auxiliary self-supervised contrastive signals operate across embedding, node, and sequence layers to simultaneously refine item discriminability and global user preferences alongside primary cross-entropy training. On Amazon Sports, Beauty, and Toys benchmarks, MLGCL-SR surpasses leading baselines, achieving NDCG@10 improvements of 14.2%, 19.1%, and 23.1% over MCLRec.
## Hierarchical Transition Graph Construction and Bidirectional Message Passing

Conventional sequential recommendation models typically rely on unidirectional recurrent architectures or self-attention mechanisms that process interaction histories as flat sequences. When interaction graphs are sparse, these models fail to capture complex item transition patterns. MLGCL-SR addresses this limitation by transforming chronological user click sequences into structured item transition graphs. An optimized collaborative filtering similarity function penalizes dominant high-frequency items to establish reliable transitions for single-interaction cold-start items.

The core representation backbone, designated BI-SRGNN, employs an optimized Bidirectional Gated Graph Neural Network (BI-GGNN). Unlike standard GNNs that propagate messages solely in the forward temporal direction, BI-GGNN performs forward message aggregation, reverses directed edge orientations, and executes backward message aggregation. The resulting forward and backward representations are linearly transformed, concatenated, and fed into a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) module alongside historical hidden states across 3 stacked layers with a scale factor of 15 and dropout of 0.3. This mechanism enriches node embeddings with preceding and succeeding context before sequence-level attention pooling.
- Penalized item similarity metric mitigates popularity bias during single-item positive pair construction.
- Bidirectional edge traversal allows each interaction node to synthesize past and future sequential dependencies.
- Softmax attention combines global sequence representations with terminal item embeddings to preserve immediate user intent.
**Table (Hierarchical Transition Graph Construction and Bidirectional Message Passing)**
## Multi-Level Contrastive Auxiliary Supervision Across Representation Tiers

To prevent embedding collapse and enhance representation granularity under sparse feedback, MLGCL-SR injects self-supervised contrastive learning at three distinct structural depths: the embedding layer, the node representation layer, and the sequence representation layer. Unlike prior single-tier contrastive methods such as CL4SRec and CoSeRec, this multi-tier formulation decouples item-level semantics from trajectory-level user intent.

At the embedding and node layers, contrastive pairs are formed across adjacent items using a sliding window of size 2 over the interaction sequence, pulling immediate 1-hop transition pairs closer while treating distant hops as negatives. At the sequence level, explicit data augmentation generates dual sequence views. Controlled comparative tuning established that an augmentation pairing of item masking at ratio m=0.15 and item reordering at ratio r=0.3 achieves superior alignment without corrupting semantic intent. The resulting representations are mapped via a 3-layer MLP projector into contrastive InfoNCE loss objectives.
- Embedding and node contrastive losses refine local item embeddings and topological neighborhood structures.
- Sequence-level contrastive loss enforces stability across stochastic views generated through masking and reordering.
- Multi-task optimization balances primary cross-entropy with auxiliary contrastive losses using fixed coefficients alpha=0.9, beta=0.03, gamma=0.03, and delta=0.04.
**Table (Multi-Level Contrastive Auxiliary Supervision Across Representation Tiers)**
## Empirical Benchmark Verification and Component Ablation Dynamics

The empirical efficacy of MLGCL-SR was validated on three public Amazon e-commerce benchmarks: Sports (35,598 users, 18,357 items), Beauty (22,363 users, 12,101 items), and Toys (19,412 users, 11,924 items). Evaluation followed a leave-one-out protocol using Adam optimization with batch size 256, learning rate 0.0001, and embedding dimension 512 on an Intel Xeon Gold 6330 CPU and NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPU.

MLGCL-SR consistently outperforms baselines including CL4SRec, CoSeRec, ICLRec, DuoRec, and MCLRec. Ranking performance gains are particularly pronounced on ranking-sensitive metrics, where NDCG@5 improvements reach 20.6% on Sports, 26.7% on Beauty, and 26.2% on Toys relative to MCLRec. Ablation experiments confirm that removing all contrastive layers (MLGCL-SR-All) degrades performance substantially, while isolating individual layers reveals that node-level contrastive learning provides the strongest marginal benefit due to graph-contextualized feature refinement.
- Performance advantages expand as dataset scale decreases from Sports to Toys, demonstrating robustness in sparse regimes.
- Ablation indicates that removing sequence contrast produces minor drops on truncated histories, while removing node contrast yields larger performance degradation.
## Operational Boundary Conditions and Algorithmic Constraints
MLGCL-SR requires structural transition graph generation and manual multi-task balancing across contrastive loss components, introducing tuning complexity in high-throughput recommendation systems.
- Negative sampling and pair generation at embedding and node layers rely on fixed sliding windows of size 2, restricting local contrastive signals to immediate 1-hop adjacencies.

- Multi-task loss weighting across four coefficients (alpha=0.9, beta=0.03, gamma=0.03, delta=0.04) was determined manually, lacking automated adaptive gradient calibration across heterogeneous datasets.

Continuous monitoring of vulnerable elderly populations requires sensing systems that maintain complete visual privacy while avoiding the compliance overhead of wristbands or pendants. Optical cameras face resistance in private domestic spaces such as bedrooms and bathrooms, whereas wearable accelerometers are often forgotten or discarded. In this investigation, motion capture is conducted using a Texas Instruments IWR6843ISK frequency-modulated continuous wave radar emitting chirp signals spanning 60 GHz to 64 GHz. Transmitted signals reflect off dynamic human body segments and mix with local oscillator chirps, generating intermediate frequency signals that track micro-Doppler signatures, spatial velocities, and range profiles without capturing identifiable anatomical imagery.

To bypass the logistical impossibility and ethical hazard of having elderly individuals repeatedly stage falls, the detection task is formulated as deep anomaly detection. An encoder-decoder architecture pairs with a feature predictor trained exclusively on non-fall daily living activities. Falls represent low-probability abnormal kinetics that deviate sharply from nominal temporal feature distributions, triggering elevated anomaly scores during inference.
- Eliminates camera privacy vulnerabilities through contactless 60 GHz to 64 GHz radio frequency tracking.
- Trains purely on non-fall daily activities, avoiding risky fall data generation in older cohorts.

## Domain-Invariant Feature Alignment and Denoising Robustness

A central barrier to deploying radar anomaly detectors across disparate living facilities is domain divergence caused by varying room geometries, furniture occlusions, and diverse individual movement velocities. When applied to unfamiliar subjects, conventional distance metrics and reconstruction models suffer performance collapse. The proposed architecture counters this by introducing Maximum Mean Discrepancy alignment directly into the latent feature space, minimizing distribution variance between disparate source domains and forcing the encoder to isolate domain-invariant kinematic representations.

Complementing domain alignment, denoising learning is introduced across both the feature extractor and the latent predictor by injecting Gaussian noise into raw radar tensors and intermediate feature layers. This training noise forces the network to learn robust trajectory topologies rather than overfitting to environmental multipath artifacts. Experimental ablation demonstrates that incorporating domain alignment increases true positive rate from 91.37% to 94.29%, while joint encoder-predictor noise injection improves the base area under the curve from 0.9952 to 0.9967.
- Direction loss formulation exhibits superior sensitivity compared to standard mean squared Euclidean distance.
- Joint noise injection fortifies the latent predictor against multipath clutter and sensor drift.
**Table (Domain-Invariant Feature Alignment and Denoising Robustness)**
## Cross-Validation Benchmarks and Benchmark Generalization

The model was rigorously validated across an empirical dataset collected in ten natural indoor settings, including dormitories, offices, and lounges populated with standard furnishings. The dataset encompasses 52 non-fall daily activity categories (totaling 11 870 non-fall instances) and 12 distinct fall types (totaling 850 fall instances), supplemented by 15 720 unconstrained daily living samples from non-fall rooms. An eight-fold cross-validation protocol tested generalization onto unseen subject-environment combinations.

Using directional cosine loss as the anomaly threshold, the model achieved an average AUROC of 0.9979, a true positive rate of 96.12%, and a false positive rate of 0.97%. In contrast to baseline models such as One-Class SVM, K-Means, K-Nearest Neighbors, and 3D Convolutional Autoencoders whose performance declines sharply under domain shifts, the proposed model retained high discriminative margins. While 60 GHz to 64 GHz radar signals prevent invasion of user privacy and bypass wearable non-compliance, practical deployment is constrained by wave attenuation and line-of-sight physical barriers.

## 1. Executive Abstract

Provincial ordinary highway networks are significant contributors to transport carbon emissions, yet a standardized estimation framework remains absent. This study develops a bottom-up model to quantify vehicle carbon emissions on such networks using link traffic data (LTD). The model integrates a theoretical fuel consumption model with vehicle type, gross vehicle mass, and driving cycle parameters to achieve link-level emission resolution. A maximum entropy origin-destination (OD) inference model redistributes observed link flows to the entire network. The Bureau of Public Roads (BPR) function classifies link average speeds into free-flow and non-free-flow states, yielding speed-specific driving cycles. Fuel consumption rates are derived from the MOVES open-source database's per-second energy consumption values under corresponding cycle segments. Fuel and electricity consumption are calculated per vehicle type using cycle curves and vehicle kilometers traveled, then converted to carbon emissions via carbon balance principles. A case study of Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region for November 2019 estimates total network emissions at 195,900 tonnes. Freight vehicles dominate, contributing 87.85% of emissions, with heavy-duty trucks alone accounting for 76.47% of freight emissions. Small passenger cars contribute only 12.15% of total emissions but 82.93% of passenger car emissions. Validation against MOVES, COPERT, and provincial statistical bureau fuel consumption data confirms the model's feasibility and high accuracy. The reconstructed driving cycles are adaptable to complex Chinese road networks, providing a granular tool for provincial carbon emission management.
## 2. Core Quantitative Takeaways

- Freight vehicles account for 87.85% of total provincial ordinary highway network carbon emissions (195,900 tonnes in Ningxia, November 2019), with heavy-duty trucks alone contributing 76.47% of freight emissions-underscoring the urgent need for targeted freight decarbonization policies and fleet electrification incentives.

- Small passenger cars represent only 12.15% of total network emissions but 82.93% of passenger car emissions, indicating that passenger car emission reduction strategies must prioritize this vehicle class despite its lower overall share.

- The maximum entropy OD inference model successfully reconstructs network-wide flow distributions from limited link traffic data, achieving a relative error below 5% in traffic volume observations, which enables cost-effective emission mapping without exhaustive sensor deployment.

- Validation against MOVES and COPERT simulations and provincial statistical fuel consumption data confirms the model's high accuracy, with reconstructed driving cycles adapted from CATC series cycles proving suitable for complex Chinese road networks, avoiding the inadaptability of international emission software.

To reconcile the diverging requirements observed across heterogeneous scenarios, the empirical metric taxonomy is projected onto a tri-dimensional evaluation framework comprising Service Quality (S), Resource Multiplexing Cost (M), and Scenario Versatility (V). The S dimension assesses whether network delivery satisfies client-facing operational requirements, including throughput, jitter, and reliability. The M dimension evaluates operational cost acceptability, tracking physical infrastructure footprints across spectrum, computational overhead, and transmission energy. The V dimension evaluates dynamic programmability and structural reconfiguration cost when onboarding emerging modalities.

Under this governance model, heterogeneous traffic profiles are projected into distinct S-M operational planes. Real-time tasks with stringent delay thresholds but flexible bandwidth budgets share specialized scheduling planes, while elastic background flows occupy high-multiplexing configurations. An AI-native control plane manages inter-plane physical resource distribution while intra-plane protocols handle fine-grained packet contention. Continuous measurement of operational performance ensures adaptive expansion, consolidation, or retirement of S-M planes as operational traffic distributions evolve over time.
- Data center queue buffering operates simultaneously across S and M dimensions by influencing transmission delay while defining memory utilization.

This work presents a 12-bit 100 MS/s asynchronous pipelined successive-approximation-register (Pipelined-SAR) analog-to-digital converter fabricated in TSMC 65 nm standard CMOS at a 1.2 V supply. The converter employs a three-stage 4-bit + 4-bit + 6-bit pipeline in which each sub-ADC is a SAR stage built around a floating-inverter-based pre-amplifier (FIA) comparator, a DAC capacitor array, and SAR logic. The FIA comparator merges the two tail capacitors into a single floating reservoir capacitor CRES, creating an isolated voltage domain that forces the common-mode current into the integration capacitors to zero, thereby eliminating the common-mode feedback (CMFB) loop and achieving current reuse with roughly twice the gm/ID of a conventional dynamic latch. A resistor self-biased pseudo-differential ring amplifier serves as the inter-stage operational amplifier; a series resistor RB in the second inverter stage generates a PVT-tracking dead-zone voltage, removing the external bias circuit and reducing the second-stage inverter count from two to one. ## Three-Stage 4b+4b+6b Asynchronous Pipelined-SAR Architecture with FIA Comparators

The converter is partitioned into three cascaded SAR stages of 4, 4, and 6 bits, giving 14 raw bits before digital encoding into a 12-bit output. In the sample-and-hold phase the input is sampled directly onto the first stage's DAC capacitor array; the FIA comparator then resolves 4 bits by switching the DAC through SAR logic. The residue is amplified by a ring amplifier and handed to the second stage, which repeats the 4-bit cycle, and the second residue drives the 6-bit third stage. A decoding circuit assembles D1<A1:A4>, D2<A5:A8>, and D3<A9:A14>.

Timing is derived from the 100 MS/s rate: each stage is allotted 10 ns, split into 3 ns sampling and 7 ns quantization. The third stage must complete six comparisons within 7 ns, fixing the comparator clock CLKC at approximately 1.16 ns. Transient simulation at 1.2 V shows the comparator reaches its output decision about 450 ps after CLKC, leaving margin inside the 1.16 ns budget. A 300-point Monte Carlo offset run gives a mean offset of 109.5 µV, satisfying the 1/2 LSB offset bound for the 12-bit converter.

column1: ## Floating-Inverter Pre-Amplifier and Resistor Self-Biased Pseudo-Differential Ring Amplifier

The FIA comparator replaces the two tail capacitors of a CMOS dynamically-biased integrator with a single floating reservoir capacitor CRES, isolating the amplifier's voltage domain from the input common mode. Because the pull-up and pull-down currents are equal, the common-mode current into the integration capacitors is forced to zero, so no CMFB loop is needed and the output common mode stays at 0.6 V from the 1.2 V supply. The inverter-based input pair reuses current, giving roughly twice the gm/ID of a conventional dynamic latch at the start of integration, and the input pair self-terminates as the reservoir discharges, preventing full discharge of CX.

The inter-stage amplifier is a three-inverter ring amplifier in which a series resistor RB in the second stage develops a dynamic voltage drop during the slew phase, pushing the third stage into subthreshold and raising its output impedance so the loop settles into amplification. This drop tracks PVT, so the external dead-zone bias generator is eliminated and the second stage uses one inverter instead of two. The amplifier is pseudo-differential with switched-capacitor CMFB, avoiding a tail current source for faster settling. Simulated open-loop gain is 71 dB against a 65 dB finite-gain requirement, GBW is 3.89 GHz against 2.56 GHz, and phase margin is 62° against 60°.

Traditional automatic modulation classification methods treat IQ samples as isolated one-dimensional time-series, failing to output temporal boundaries and occupied channel bandwidths necessary for dynamic spectrum management and interference excision. The STFT configuration utilizes a sampling rate of 200 kHz, a Hanning window of length 64, an FFT size of 256, and an overlap of 60 points, generating 213x213 pixel single-channel spectrograms capturing instantaneous amplitude and phase variations.

To simulate wideband spectral monitoring where multiple non-cooperative emissions coexist, individual subgraphs are organized into 3x3 grids yielding 640x640 composite images. Stratified independent sampling without replacement ensures that adjacent sub-windows do not share signal-to-noise ratios or modulation categories. Standard YOLOv10 architectures aggregate multi-scale features through path aggregation networks by concatenating uncompressed backbone channels, forcing downstream C2f blocks to execute dimensional reduction while extracting semantic abstractions. Inside each bottleneck, input channels are partitioned with n_div=4, routing 1/4 of the channels through 3x3 convolutions while the remaining 3/4 bypass computation via identity mapping. Conventional deep image hiding techniques encode secret color distributions across standard convolutional manifolds without distinguishing between flat low-frequency textures and dense high-frequency contours. This uniform dispersion exposes carriers to statistical steganalysis, as modified smooth patches yield detectable residual artifacts. CBAM-CGAN counteracts this vulnerability by inserting serialized channel and spatial attention modules directly into the generator and extractor backbones. The channel attention mechanism isolates dominant feature responses via shared multi-layer perceptron projections across max-pooled and average-pooled representations, while the complementary spatial attention mechanism calculates inter-spatial relationships through dilated 7x7 spatial pooling.

To condition stego generation upon specific host traits, the generator incorporates two initial convolutional operations that project the 256x256 cover image into conditioning label tensor TC. This conditional feature map enters the concatenation pipeline alongside raw secret image M and cover image C. Network optimization relies on a dual-loop adversarial scheme: the generator minimizes combined mean squared error distortion L1, extraction feedback loss L3, and adversarial evasion loss L2 against a dedicated XuNet steganalyzer. Simultaneously, the extractor reconstructs secret image M' guided by pixel MSE, VGG16 relu2_2 perceptual loss, and an auxiliary four-layer convolutional discriminator that enforces output indistinguishability from ground-truth secret distributions.

External vulnerability knowledge is increasingly important for large language models (LLMs) to understand vulnerability targets, craft exploit payloads, and interpret verification evidence. Recent approaches incorporate external vulnerability knowledge via prompt, task planning and multi-agent collaboration to improve automated penetration testing. However, automated vulnerability reproduction remains challenging because public exploit materials are heterogeneous and loosely structured, spanning scripts, HTTP requests, command-line snippets, and walkthroughs in natural language. Prior work has leveraged retrieval-augmented generation, PoC semantic repair, and exploit code generation, but still constrained by environment dependencies, exploit semantic extraction and model hallucinations, weakening the trustworthiness of automated reproduction. To address these issues, we propose ValidPoC, an LLM-driven framework for automated vulnerability reproduction that converts heterogeneous exploit walkthroughs or scripts into structured and reliable PoC-Nuclei templates. ValidPoC defines a PoC semantic model that provides a unified representation of exploit logic, including request construction, payload generation, execution dependencies, and verification criteria. We develop a Semgrep-assisted semantic parsing mechanism to extract PoC Semantic IR from public exploit materials, including exploit scripts and natural-language descriptions, and construct structured Nuclei YAML templates for automated vulnerability reproduction. To improve reproduction reliability, we establish a closed-loop execution-evaluation-feedback optimization mechanism with layered L1-L3 verification. Experiments on the Vulhub dataset show that ValidPoC achieves 76.12% Pass@3, outperforming PentestAgent by 4.48 percentage points, while reducing average time by 1.62x and token consumption by 54.79%.

ValidPoC addresses the bottleneck of converting heterogeneous public exploit materials—Python/Ruby scripts, HTTP requests, and natural-language walkthroughs—into standardized, executable PoC-Nuclei templates. By defining a PoC semantic model and using Semgrep-assisted parsing to extract a Semantic IR, the framework reduces environment dependencies and model hallucinations that plague prior LLM-based penetration testing agents. The closed-loop execution-evaluation-feedback mechanism with L1-L3 layered verification ensures that generated templates are not only syntactically valid but also trigger the vulnerability with observable evidence.

On the Vulhub dataset, ValidPoC achieves 76.12% Pass@3, outperforming PentestAgent by 4.48 percentage points while cutting average execution time by 1.62x and token consumption by 54.79%. The ablation study shows that removing the semantic parsing and template generation mechanism collapses Pass@3 to 29.85%, underscoring the importance of structured intermediate representation. The approach is best suited for request-driven, evidence-observable vulnerabilities; it is limited by Nuclei's expressiveness for session-dependent or callback-heavy exploits, where Metasploit-style dynamic state management is required.
## PoC Semantic IR and Semgrep-Assisted Template Generation

ValidPoC introduces a PoC semantic model that unifies exploit logic across request construction, payload generation, execution dependencies, and verification criteria. A Semgrep-assisted semantic parsing mechanism extracts a PoC Semantic IR from public exploit materials, including Python and Ruby scripts as well as natural-language descriptions. This IR is then transformed into structured Nuclei YAML templates. The parsing leverages Semgrep's pattern-matching capabilities to identify key code constructs such as HTTP request libraries, command execution calls, and parameter assignments, enabling robust extraction even from loosely structured scripts. The resulting templates encode request methods, paths, headers, payloads, and matchers in a standardized format, reducing the need for manual adaptation and minimizing environment-specific dependencies.

The template generation process is guided by task-specific prompts that instruct the LLM to map IR components to Nuclei syntax. For example, payload generation logic is translated into raw HTTP requests with dynamic variables such as {{interactsh-url}} and {{marker}}, while verification criteria become matchers-condition blocks combining word, status, and interactsh_protocol checks. This structured approach ensures that generated templates are syntactically valid and semantically faithful to the original exploit. The framework also incorporates payload safety checks, downgrading high-risk post-exploitation actions (e.g., trojan downloads) to benign system information queries while preserving the vulnerability trigger logic, thereby reducing the risk of public PoC contamination.

## Layered L1-L3 Verification and Closed-Loop Feedback Optimization

ValidPoC establishes a closed-loop execution-evaluation-feedback optimization mechanism with three verification layers: L1 checks template syntax and structural validity against Nuclei scanner rules; L2 verifies that the template triggers the expected response or interaction; and L3 confirms the actual security impact through multi-source evidence such as callback records, file changes, or command execution output. The evaluation agent analyzes execution logs to diagnose failures, and the template repair agent adjusts trigger parameters, request formats, and verification evidence accordingly. This iterative process continues until the template passes L3 or a maximum iteration limit is reached.

On the Vulhub dataset, this mechanism raises Pass@1 from 41.79% to Pass@3 of 76.12%, a 34.33 percentage point improvement, demonstrating the effectiveness of feedback-driven repair. The ablation study shows that removing the layered verification and feedback optimization drops RL1 to 100% but Pass@3 to 29.85%, indicating that without L3-level evidence, templates may pass superficial checks but fail to prove actual exploitation. The framework also achieves a false match rate (FMR) of 8.96%, significantly lower than the 19.40% of community Nuclei templates, because it avoids weak matching rules such as status code or version fingerprint alone.

## Nuclei Expressiveness Boundaries and Environment-Specific Constraints

## 1. Executive Abstract

External vulnerability knowledge is increasingly important for large language models (LLMs) to understand vulnerability targets, craft exploit payloads, and interpret verification evidence. Recent approaches incorporate external vulnerability knowledge via prompt, task planning and multi-agent collaboration to improve automated penetration testing. However, automated vulnerability reproduction remains challenging because public exploit materials are heterogeneous and loosely structured, spanning scripts, HTTP requests, command-line snippets, and walkthroughs in natural language. Prior work has leveraged retrieval-augmented generation, PoC semantic repair, and exploit code generation, but still constrained by environment dependencies, exploit semantic extraction and model hallucinations, weakening the trustworthiness of automated reproduction. To address these issues, we propose ValidPoC, an LLM-driven framework for automated vulnerability reproduction that converts heterogeneous exploit walkthroughs or scripts into structured and reliable PoC-Nuclei templates. ValidPoC defines a PoC semantic model that provides a unified representation of exploit logic, including request construction, payload generation, execution dependencies, and verification criteria. We develop a Semgrep-assisted semantic parsing mechanism to extract PoC Semantic IR from public exploit materials, including exploit scripts and natural-language descriptions, and construct structured Nuclei YAML templates for automated vulnerability reproduction. To improve reproduction reliability, we establish a closed-loop execution-evaluation-feedback optimization mechanism with layered L1-L3 verification. Experiments on the Vulhub dataset show that ValidPoC achieves 76.12% Pass@3, outperforming PentestAgent by 4.48 percentage points, while reducing average time by 1.62x and token consumption by 54.79%.

- The layered L1-L3 verification and feedback optimization raise reproduction success from Pass@1 41.79% to Pass@3 76.12%, a 34.33 percentage point gain.
- Ablation removing PoC semantic parsing and template generation drops RL1 to 76.12% and Pass@3 to 29.85%, confirming the mechanism's necessity.

Conventional deep learning pest classification systems frequently struggle in natural farmland environments due to severe canopy occlusion, high inter-class visual similarity, and drastic structural shifts across insect metamorphosis. Public datasets like IP102 have supported benchmark progress, yet they lack granular coverage of developmental instars, perspective diversity, and extreme scale disparities. To resolve these limitations, this investigation introduces the Agricultural Pest Multi-dimensional Dataset (APMD), comprising 15 680 images across 58 agricultural pest species spanning 8 orders (Hemiptera, Lepidoptera, Coleoptera, Diptera, Hymenoptera, Acari, Orthoptera, and Isoptera). The dataset systematically records complete life cycles across holometabolous species (egg, larva, pupa, adult) and hemimetabolous species (egg, nymph, adult), spanning physical scales from minute pests under 1 mm to mature specimens exceeding 30 mm.

Built upon the Multi-granularity Part Sampling Attention (MPSA) baseline, DFS-PestNet adopts a Swin-B backbone organized into a decoupled parallel architecture comprising a primary feature stream and a prompt-augmented stream. In the deep Stage4 feature extraction phase, a Spatial Dependency Perception (SDP) mechanism models structural shifts. Meanwhile, across shallow-to-intermediate Stage1 through Stage3 representations, the prompt-augmented stream introduces explicit category semantics and spatial localization tokens via the Advanced Haptic-Visual Prompting (AHVP) module, preventing feature degradation across life stages.
- Curated APMD benchmark partitions 15 680 images into training (10 962), validation (3 132), and testing (1 566) subsets.
- Decoupled parallel processing preserves raw hierarchical representations while injecting life-stage semantic guidance.
**Table (Multidimensional Agricultural Dataset and Dual-Stream Decoupled Architecture)**
## Adaptive Spatial Deformation and Life-Cycle Semantic Prompting Mechanisms

Fine-grained insect recognition demands localized modeling of discriminative anatomical structures such as wing venation, spot configurations, and antennae. The SDP module processes Stage4 feature tensors through dual parallel pathways: an upper spatial deformation branch and a lower heatmap branch. The deformation branch computes coordinate displacement fields using 1x1 and 3x3 convolutions, directing a stride-2 3x3 deformable convolution layer to sample irregularly shaped insect contours. Concurrently, the heatmap branch applies 3x3 depthwise separable convolutions and GeLU activations to produce spatial attention weights, which downsample via bilinear interpolation to residually modulate sampled feature activations.

To mitigate visual feature confusion caused by larval, pupal, and imaginal polymorphism, the AHVP module injects prompt tokens into Stage1 to Stage3 layers. Spatial guidance is established by projecting 2D normalized coordinate grids and computing Euclidean distances against V learnable prompt center coordinates. In parallel, global context vectors pass through multi-layer perceptron gating layers to modulate 512-dimensional class semantic embeddings, generating prompt-enhanced feature representations that align multi-stage morphological invariants.
- SDP residual modulation incorporates a learnable scaling parameter alpha, suppressing background clutter while amplifying diagnostic features.
- AHVP gating coefficients dynamically calibrate semantic influence across individual spatial coordinates.
**Table (Adaptive Spatial Deformation and Life-Cycle Semantic Prompting Mechanisms)**
## Dual-Branch Saliency Sampling and Comprehensive Benchmark Validation

Identifying miniature agricultural pests, such as leafhopper nymphs and stem-boring larvae, typically fails under standard attention pooling due to resolution loss. The Dual-branch Saliency Sampling (DSS) module replaces conventional part sampling by deploying parallel lightweight networks composed of linear layers and GeLU activations. The primary branch predicts global salient foreground regions, while a specialized small-target branch isolates localized, high-frequency discriminative features. Both branches combine through sigmoid-gated interpolation to construct an attention bias that adjusts prototype query matrices before Softmax normalization.

Rigorous ablation on IP102 confirms that integrating SDP, AHVP, and DSS elevates accuracy from 75.03% to 77.24%, precision from 67.85% to 71.64%, recall from 64.60% to 68.78%, and F1-score from 66.18% to 70.18%. Systematic parameter sweeps identify optimal stability at 6 prompt position tokens and a feature dropout rate of 0.2. In cross-model benchmarks, DFS-PestNet outperforms leading CNN and vision transformer baselines, achieving 98.01% accuracy on APMD and 77.24% on IP102 while delivering inference throughputs of 164 frame/s and 158 frame/s, respectively.
- DSS prototypes steer attention distribution across discriminative keypoints, eliminating misclassification of miniature pests.
- t-SNE dimensionality reduction verifies enhanced inter-class separation and tighter intra-class clustering across disparate instars.

Agricultural pest monitoring in real-world farmland environments is severely challenged by background clutter, drastic morphological shifts across developmental instars, diverse imaging angles, and broad scale spans. Addressing these limitations, researchers constructed the Agricultural Pest Multi-dimensional Dataset (APMD) comprising 15 680 images across 58 species and introduced DFS-PestNet, a decoupled parallel vision architecture built upon Swin-B. The framework integrates a Spatial Dependency Perception module for dynamic deformation modeling, an Advanced Haptic-Visual Prompting module for injecting semantic priors, and a Dual-branch Saliency Sampling module for capturing minute targets. On IP102 and APMD benchmarks, DFS-PestNet attained top-tier accuracies of 77.24% and 98.01% alongside throughputs of 158 frame/s and 164 frame/s.
## Operational Boundary Conditions and Future Deployment Constraints
While DFS-PestNet demonstrates high accuracy and throughput on structured benchmarks, practical deployment in wild agricultural edge setups presents clear architectural constraints.
- Edge hardware constraints necessitate future model lightweighting to adapt the Swin-B backbone from RTX 4060 GPU environments to low-power embedded monitoring terminals.

- Closed-set classification assumes all field-observed specimens belong to known taxonomic classes, highlighting the need for open-set recognition to detect and flag previously unencountered invasive species.

We propose a multi-level image fusion method that operates across three hierarchical tiers: pixel, feature, and decision levels. At the pixel level, an initial fusion enhances the detection model's sensitivity to texture and morphological details. At the feature level, a deeper fusion steers the model toward global semantic information, capturing target characteristics in complex backgrounds. At the decision level, fused information is integrated to select detection results with high confidence and precision. This work provides a viable pathway for multi-modal remote sensing image analysis, with potential extensions to latency-sensitive edge deployment and large-scale heterogeneous sensor networks.","[""Multi-level integration across pixel, feature, and decision hierarchies achieves precision rates of 97.1% for cars, 97.8% for ships, and 98.9% for airplanes."", ""The proposed method suppresses detection miss rates to 11.2% for cars, 11.3% for ships, and 11.5% for airplanes, maintaining an average miss rate below 11.5% across all classes."", ""Ablation testing on vehicle recognition reveals that removing the pixel-level fusion tier reduces mean cosine similarity from 0.915 to 0.887, confirming the importance of low-level texture preservation."", ""Removing the feature-level fusion tier causes mean cosine similarity to drop to 0.892, underscoring the critical function of dual-phase local and global channel attention."", ""The benchmark dataset establishes 1,128 paired SAR and visible light images encompassing 2,128 annotated target objects across shore, land, and sea environments.""]",5,"## Hierarchical Cross-Modal Architecture and Multi-Tier Fusion Formulation

The integrated neural network processes paired three-channel SAR and visible light images through three sequential operational hierarchies: pixel-level fusion, feature-level fusion, and decision-level integration. At the initial tier, preprocessed SAR and optical inputs are stacked along the channel dimension into a six-channel tensor. A 1x1 convolution followed by batch normalization and ReLU activation projects this representation back into a three-channel fused image, sharpening target geometry and edge details while retaining environmental context.

The fused image, alongside the original SAR and visible light inputs, enters a shared ResNet101 backbone coupled with a Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) and Region Proposal Network (RPN). The resulting multi-scale representations undergo two-stage feature fusion. In stage one, optical and SAR feature maps are concatenated and compressed with a channel reduction ratio r=2, applying local spatial convolution and sigmoid weighting to extract local context. In stage two, global average pooling compresses spatial dimensions into C-dimensional channel descriptors, where secondary convolution and sigmoid gating generate global attention weights. Two parallel detection streams emerge: Path 1 processes multi-scale features focused on global semantic context, while Path 2 processes pixel-fused features tuned to fine morphological cues.
- Channel compression factor r=2 controls intermediate feature dimensionality within both attention stages.
- Region of Interest (ROI) extraction and pooling feed parallel multilayer perceptron classification and regression encoders.
- Joint network optimization utilizes a multitask loss combining cross-entropy classification and smooth L1 bounding box regression.
**Table (Hierarchical Cross-Modal Architecture and Multi-Tier Fusion Formulation)**
## Empirical Target Recognition Benchmarks and Baseline Comparison

Experimental validation was conducted on a curated multimodal benchmark comprising 1,128 registered SAR and optical image pairs partitioned into 902 training pairs and 226 testing pairs (a 4:1 split). The dataset contains 2,128 target instances across 556 land scenes, 328 shore scenes, and 244 sea surface scenes, with object bounding boxes ranging from 6x12 pixels up to 128x63 pixels across car (988 objects), ship (672 objects), and airplane (468 objects) categories.

When evaluated against four established multimodal detection algorithms, the multi-level architecture achieved lower miss rates and higher precision across every category. Specifically, vehicle detection achieved 97.1% precision with an 11.2% miss rate, maritime vessel detection attained 97.8% precision with an 11.3% miss rate, and aircraft detection reached 98.9% precision with an 11.5% miss rate. Across all three categories, the proposed architecture sustained an average miss rate below 11.5% while holding precision above 97%, outperforming single-tier and dual-tier baselines.
- Maintains precision gains between 0.7% and 1.7% over the highest-performing published baseline across tested categories.
- Reduces target miss rates by 0.9% for vehicles, 0.9% for ships, and 1.0% for aircraft relative to the strongest comparative baseline.
**Table (Empirical Target Recognition Benchmarks and Baseline Comparison)**
## Dual-Stream Decision Arbitration and Modular Ablation Dynamics

The decision-level fusion module reconciles candidate predictions generated by Path 1 and Path 2. If the predicted class labels between the two paths diverge, the framework directly outputs the detection associated with higher confidence. When predicted class labels match, the module evaluates the Intersection over Union (IoU) of the bounding boxes. For overlapping boxes exceeding an IoU threshold of 0.5, predictions are identified as a unified object; when IoU falls below 0.5, the final bounding box coordinates are determined through a confidence-weighted average combining the two candidate boxes.

Ablation experiments evaluated vehicle recognition accuracy using cosine similarity metrics across four configurations: complete architecture, complete architecture without pixel-level fusion, without feature-level fusion, and without decision-level fusion. Omitting pixel-level fusion caused the largest performance degradation, decreasing the mean cosine similarity from 0.915 to 0.887 and minimum similarity from 0.869 to 0.845. Removing feature-level fusion dropped mean similarity to 0.892, while omitting decision-level arbitration yielded a mean similarity of 0.905. These findings demonstrate that low-level textural synthesis and intermediate semantic attention serve as primary drivers of detection fidelity, while decision-level arbitration eliminates residual bounding box ambiguities.

Remote sensing target recognition using synthetic aperture radar (SAR) and visible light imagery frequently suffers from information loss and detail blurring during cross-modal integration. To resolve these challenges, this study develops an integrated end-to-end framework coupling pixel-level, feature-level, and decision-level fusion tiers. The architecture employs pixel concatenation to preserve fine textures, dual-phase local and global attention modules to capture multi-scale semantic contexts, and an IoU-guided decision mechanism to reconcile multi-path bounding box proposals. Evaluated on 1,128 paired multimodal images derived from QXS-SAROPT, the framework achieves precision rates exceeding 97% and miss rates below 11.5% across vehicle, ship, and aircraft categories.
## Operational Boundary Conditions and Dataset Constraints

## Lightweight Residual Encoding and Illumination Distribution Modulation

In degraded optical environments, strided downsampling operations typically discard critical high-frequency textures and edge gradients. LRBDU-Net counteracts this degradation in its U-shaped encoder through the Lightweight Residual Feature Extraction (LRFE) unit. Implemented across every two downsampling steps, LRFE subjects the shallow feature tensor X to max pooling, reducing spatial resolution to one-fourth, followed by a 1x1 pointwise convolution that matches channels to 4C. Adding this aligned projection directly to deep intermediate features mitigates information decay without introducing heavy multi-layer subnets.

At the encoder-decoder bottleneck, the Brightness-aware Deep Semantic feature Processing (BDSP) module models non-uniform illumination fields. After Layer Normalization, the BrightAware sub-unit computes global average pooling and global maximum pooling across channel axes, extracting mean and peak illumination representations. These descriptors pass through shared 1x1 convolutions and a Sigmoid activation to generate channel-wise brightness distribution weights. The calibrated tensor is subsequently processed through depthwise separable convolutions for spatial pattern capture and Squeeze-and-Excitation (SEBlock) attention for channel prioritization before residual re-injection.
- LRFE applies max pooling and 1x1 pointwise convolution to align shallow spatial dimensions with deep feature channels.
- BDSP integrates global average and maximum pooling to establish illumination priors, preventing localized overexposure.
- SEBlock and depthwise separable convolutions coordinate dual-domain spatial-channel feature extraction.
**Table (Lightweight Residual Encoding and Illumination Distribution Modulation)**
## Dynamic Gated Decoding and Perception Color Hybrid Optimization

Standard U-Net decoders rely on static channel concatenation between skip connections and upsampled feature maps, frequently propagating amplified background noise into restored layers. LRBDU-Net replaces naive concatenation with Dynamic Feature Fusion (DFF). The module concatenates encoder and decoder feature maps into a composite representation of dimension H x W x 2C, derives adaptive channel weights via global average pooling and pointwise convolutions, reduces channel dimensionality, and scales features through spatial attention maps generated from twin 1x1 convolutions and Sigmoid gating.

To suppress network complexity, LRBDU-Net constructs its core convolutional stages using Group and Ghost (GpGh) convolutions. Group convolutions subdivide input channels into G disjoint subsets to curtail arithmetic operations, while Ghost convolutions generate primary intrinsic feature maps using pointwise operators and derive secondary feature maps via cheap linear group convolutions. Optimization is driven by a Perception-Color Hybrid (PCH) objective combining pixel-level L1 loss, a VGG19 perceptual loss utilizing the first 16 layers, and a multi-channel color difference penalty.

- GpGh hybrid blocks lower parameter and FLOP requirements by combining group division and linear ghost transformations.
- PCH loss couples L1 reconstruction with pre-trained 16-layer VGG19 perceptual discrepancies and inter-channel color variance.
