Online aggregation queries over high-volume streaming data demand exact, low-latency responses on embedded devices whose RAM is typically limited to 128 MB–1 GB. Conventional segment trees require several times the storage of the original data, making them impractical in such resource-constrained settings. This work introduces the Subspace Segment Tree, which partitions the tree into three hierarchical layers—solid, dynamic, and imaginary—delimited by depth thresholds D1 and D2. Solid-layer nodes remain permanently resident, imaginary-layer nodes are never materialized and are computed on demand, and dynamic-layer nodes are activated and destroyed through a fixed-size memory pool governed by least-recently-used (LRU) eviction. Across D1 values from 1 to 18, the structure reduces node count from 1,506,974 (plain segment tree) to approximately 146,011 nodes, achieving 90.31% spatial optimization at D1 = 1–13 while query cost falls from 3.06 s to 2.61 s at D1 = 15 (14.62% time improvement). Under phase-changing workloads, average query time decreases from 0.0222 ms (D1 = 8) to 0.0162 ms (D1 = 14) with zero destructions; under volatile-alternating workloads, destructions range from 24,892 to 33,169 and average query time falls from 0.0875 ms to 0.0523 ms. The mechanism preserves exact aggregation semantics while bounding index memory via D1 and D2.

Embedded streaming databases must return exact aggregation results within RAM budgets of 128 MB–1 GB, yet a plain segment tree consumes roughly ten times the node count of the proposed index (1,506,974 versus 146,011 nodes). The Subspace Segment Tree resolves this by keeping only the upper solid layer permanently resident, computing imaginary-layer nodes on demand, and cycling dynamic-layer nodes through a fixed memory pool with LRU eviction. The trade-off is controlled by depth thresholds D1 and D2: a larger D1 lowers activation overhead and query latency but raises baseline memory, while a smaller D1 maximizes space savings at the cost of more dynamic activations.

Measured on an Intel i9-12900H with 32 GB DDR5, the structure holds 90.31% spatial optimization across D1 = 1–13 and improves query time by up to 14.62% at D1 = 15. Workload stability dominates the cost profile: phase-changing queries incur zero destructions, whereas volatile-alternating queries trigger up to 33,169 evictions and roughly triple average query latency. The lightweight LRU management and tunable footprint make the index applicable to ARM Cortex-A-class processors and eMMC/SPI Flash storage, though allocator fragmentation and long-term memory stability remain unmeasured on device.
## Three-Layer Subspace Segment Tree with Memory-Pool LRU Reclamation

The index partitions a segment tree of depth D into three layers using thresholds D1 and D2 with 0 < D1 < D2 < D. Nodes at depth 0 < d ≤ D1 form the solid layer and are permanently recorded in memory; nodes at D1 < d ≤ D2 form the dynamic layer and support activation and destruction; nodes at D2 < d ≤ D form the imaginary layer, which is never materialized and is computed on the spot when queried. A fixed-size memory pool serves dynamic-layer nodes, with occupancy priority determined by the last-use timestamp. When the pool is exhausted, the least-recently-used dynamic node is destroyed to release space for newly constructed nodes.

The aggregation semantics rest on distributed aggregation functions f defined by an initial computation g, a merge function h, and a zero element z, satisfying f(S) = g(x) for single-element sequences and h(S1.S2) = h(f(S1).f(S2)) for concatenation. Table 1 specifies g and h for sum (g(x) = x, h = f(S1) + f(S2), z = 0), max (g(x) = x, h = max(f(S1), f(S2)), z = −∞), count (g(x) = 1, h = f(S1) + f(S2), z = 0), and sum of squares (g(x) = x², h = f(S1) + f(S2), z = 0). The choice of D1 governs the central trade-off: a larger D1 keeps more upper nodes resident, reducing activation overhead for fine-grained queries but raising baseline memory, while a smaller D1 improves space savings at the cost of more dynamic activations.

## 1. Executive Abstract

Online aggregation queries over high-volume streaming data demand exact, low-latency responses on embedded devices whose RAM is typically limited to 128 MB-1 GB. Conventional segment trees require several times the storage of the original data, making them impractical in such resource-constrained settings. This work introduces the Subspace Segment Tree, which partitions the tree into three hierarchical layers-solid, dynamic, and imaginary-delimited by depth thresholds D1 and D2. Solid-layer nodes remain permanently resident, imaginary-layer nodes are never materialized and are computed on demand, and dynamic-layer nodes are activated and destroyed through a fixed-size memory pool governed by least-recently-used (LRU) eviction. Across D1 values from 1 to 18, the structure reduces node count from 1,506,974 (plain segment tree) to approximately 146,011 nodes, achieving 90.31% spatial optimization at D1 = 1-13 while query cost falls from 3.06 s to 2.61 s at D1 = 15 (14.62% time improvement). Under phase-changing workloads, average query time decreases from 0.0222 ms (D1 = 8) to 0.0162 ms (D1 = 14) with zero destructions; under volatile-alternating workloads, destructions range from 24,892 to 33,169 and average query time falls from 0.0875 ms to 0.0523 ms. The mechanism preserves exact aggregation semantics while bounding index memory via D1 and D2.

- Query cost time falls from 3.06 s (plain tree) to 2.61 s at D1 = 15, a 14.62% time improvement; D1 = 1 incurs a 20.05% time penalty (3.68 s).

- Spatial optimization degrades beyond D1 = 15: 89.72% at D1 = 16, 87.39% at D1 = 17, and 80.94% at D1 = 18 (287,257 nodes).

## Reinforcement Feedback and Progressive Multimodal Noise Gating

In unstructured social media posts, visual content frequently introduces severe cross-modal interference when images are purely decorative, abstract, or metaphoric. Conventional MNER architectures that implement global cross-modal attention often overfit to irrelevant visual artifacts, erroneously shifting textual entity spans and assigning incorrect types. To enforce reliable cross-modal grounding, RFAL constructs an image-text noise filtering (INF) layer structured around a three-stage chain-of-thought (COT) reasoning protocol driven by GPT-4o.

The filtering mechanism systematically scores image-text concordance across three hierarchical dimensions. In Stage 1, spatial relation verification extracts positional tokens and visual coordinates, outputting a discrete alignment score from 0 to 40. In Stage 2, entity-level alignment calculates TF-IDF statistics scaled by type priorities to weight fine-grained visual existence probabilities, producing an intermediate score between 0 and 40. In Stage 3, logical coherence is quantified (0 to 20) by extracting causal entity-state graphs and computing the geometric mean of node overlap and hybrid edge similarity.

The composite score S is evaluated through a dual-threshold decision function calibrated on 100 human-annotated gold standard instances. Hard thresholds guarantee the exclusion of overt discordance, while a soft margin defines an exponential probability decay buffer where retention probability scales with score proximity to the decision boundary. This probabilistic gating prevents gradient starvation and isolates downstream sequence labeling from non-descriptive visual noise.
- Stage 1 Spatial Score: Assigns 40 points for full spatial alignment, 20 points for partial match, and 0 points otherwise.
- Stage 2 Entity Alignment: Integrates TF-IDF normalized importance with entity existence confidence scores up to 40 points.
- Stage 3 Causal Graph Matching: Evaluates topological Jaccard overlap and semantic similarity across causal predicate edges.

## Adaptive Multi-Type Loss Optimization and Boundary Harmonization

Textual inputs in social corpora frequently exhibit entity boundary truncation and semantic polysemy, such as confusing commercial brand names with geographic entities. Standard cross-entropy optimization struggles under skewed class distributions, allowing high-frequency labels to dominate learning while neglecting hard tail categories. RFAL resolves this optimization imbalance by deploying an adaptive multi-type loss optimization (AMLO) layer during full fine-tuning of the Qwen2-VL-7B foundation multimodal model.

The AMLO module combines four complementary loss formulations. A class-balanced focal cross-entropy loss introduces dynamic category weighting and focusing parameters to prevent high-frequency background tokens from suppressing hard, ambiguous samples. A symmetric Kullback-Leibler divergence objective incorporates label smoothing to curb overconfident probability estimation. To rectify entity boundary fragmentation, an implicit boundary consistency loss inspects L1 distance variations across contiguous token probability vectors, penalizing divergence when neighboring tokens share identical gold tags.

Global semantic consistency is further enforced via a contrastive loss objective, which pulls representations of identical entity classes toward running cluster centroids while repelling disparate types under cosine distance normalization. The four loss terms are dynamically weighted through adaptive backpropagation parameters constrained to unit sum, ensuring balanced multi-task parameter convergence across distinct entity categories.
- Focal Loss Formulation: Employs category weights and focusing power to emphasize hard tail instances near decision boundaries.
- Symmetric KL Divergence: Integrates smoothed label targets with epsilon of 0.1 to regularize overconfident misclassifications.
- Implicit Boundary Regularization: Tracks contiguous token probability distance to penalize nested conflicts and truncated spans.
- Dynamic Weighting Initialization: Initializes loss weights from a zero-mean Gaussian distribution with variance 0.1 squared.
**Table (Adaptive Multi-Type Loss Optimization and Boundary Harmonization)**
## Empirical Verification Across Social Media Benchmarks

RFAL was comprehensively evaluated against standard sequence taggers, text-only transformers, and competitive multimodal architectures on the Twitter-2015 and Twitter-2017 datasets. Training was conducted across four Nvidia GeForce RTX 4090 GPUs using a batch size of 4, 6 training epochs, a learning rate of 1E-5, a warmup ratio of 0.03, and bfloat16 mixed-precision acceleration. Performance was assessed under strict BIO2 exact match criteria across Person (PER), Location (LOC), Organization (ORG), and Miscellaneous (MISC) categories.

Experimental metrics highlight substantial performance leads over baseline architectures. On Twitter-2015, RFAL achieved an overall F1 score of 86.45%, outperforming text-only BERT-CRF by 14.64 F1 points and surpassing the multimodal MAF baseline by 13.03 F1 points. On Twitter-2017, RFAL attained 93.80% F1, marking gains of 10.36 points over BERT-CRF and 7.55 points over MAF. Relative to advanced generation-guided architectures like PGIM and DPE-MNER, RFAL maintained solid F1 advantages across both datasets.

Ablation configurations systematically quantify the operational necessity of each architectural component. Discarding the INF module causes F1 reductions of 0.98 points on Twitter-2015 and 0.20 points on Twitter-2017, while eliminating the AMLO layer reduces F1 scores by 1.67 and 1.05 points respectively. Simultaneous removal of both mechanisms precipitates severe degradation to 83.90% and 90.79% F1, verifying that visual noise filtering and adaptive loss regularization operate synergistically.

## Operational Boundary Conditions and Computational Complexity
RFAL relies on coordinated multi-stage prompting and parameter-heavy foundation models, imposing specific deployment constraints in high-throughput environments.
- The three-stage reasoning filter introduces external API inference overhead via GPT-4o, limiting sub-second processing during large-scale real-time social data ingestion.

Gigapixel whole slide imaging exhibits severe spatial sparsity of diagnostic hallmarks, wherein positive pathological lesions occupy a tiny percentage of tissue area. Preceding pseudo-bag frameworks, such as DTFD-MIL, depend on random instance sampling to partition large bags into smaller computational units. When applied to sparse positive bags, random sampling repeatedly creates subsets devoid of tumor patches yet bearing positive slide labels, degrading the bag signal-to-noise ratio and disrupting optimization stability.

To resolve label degradation and extraneous background interference, HFMIL integrates an attention-based pseudo-bag division (APBD) mechanism. The network applies three gated attention modules over low-resolution ResNet-50 instance representations to construct class activation mappings. After computing class confidence ranks, instances residing in the bottom 10% of attention scores are discarded as non-informative background. The remaining candidate positive tiles are ranked, and high-scoring instances are systematically allocated across generated pseudo-bags before remaining instances are assigned, maintaining verifiable positive contents across bags.
- Applies Otsu thresholding to contour valid tissue zones prior to 256x256 patch extraction at 10x and 40x equivalents.
- Maps low-magnification patch coordinates (xk, yk) directly to 16 high-magnification sub-patches across coordinate grids.
- Employs dual-stage filtering discarding the bottom 10% background representations to protect pseudo-bag signal purity.

## Dual-Branch Cross-Attention Architecture and Latency Profile

Conventional multi-scale histopathology workflows typically depend on straightforward concatenation of coarse and fine embeddings, failing to align low-resolution tissue architectural topology with high-resolution cellular cytopathology. HFMIL implements a cross-attention module that takes top discriminative low-resolution queries and computes scaled dot-product attention against high-resolution keys and values. The resulting cross-attended multi-scale representation is concatenated with gated-attention pooled high-resolution bag features.

The complete network is supervised end-to-end via a dual-branch cross-entropy objective that concurrently balances low-resolution preliminary predictions and final multi-scale outputs under identical ground-truth targets. Despite the increased structural depth, HFMIL maintains real-time clinical feasibility: test profiling on an NVIDIA TITAN V 12 GB environment recorded an average inference runtime of 2.249 ms per slide representation with 2356 MB memory usage, markedly lower than the 6.620 ms and 10114 MB demanded by TransMIL.
- Integrates low-resolution gated-attention vector ti,low with high-resolution vector ti,high through learned projections.
- Operates with Adam/SGD parameterization: initial learning rate 0.001, weight decay 1e-4, momentum 0.9, and batch size 1.
- Enforces early stopping criteria with patience set to 20 epochs and minimum progression threshold at 40 epochs.

Weakly supervised classification of gigapixel whole slide images is frequently hindered by sparse diagnostic lesions, inaccurate pseudo-bag labeling, and superficial multi-scale feature concatenation. This study proposes Hierarchical Fusion Multiple Instance Learning (HFMIL). The architecture pairs attention-based pseudo-bag division (APBD) with cross-attention feature fusion across multi-resolution tiers (10x low-magnification and 40x high-magnification). ## Computational Complexity and Methodological Constraints
Although HFMIL achieves state-of-the-art diagnostic discrimination, structural constraints remain in feature preprocessing overhead and coordinate-dependent multi-magnification indexing.
- Extracting concurrent multi-scale feature embeddings using ResNet-50 increases offline tile preprocessing time and storage demands relative to single-scale patch extraction.
- Fixed coordinate geometric mapping assumes strict spatial registration between 10x and 40x image levels, limiting direct plug-and-play utility on file formats lacking pyramid hierarchies.

## Downstream Correction Benchmarks and Model Evaluation

The diagnostic and grammatical correction utility of HCGEC was evaluated using standard MaxMatch (M2) metrics against established baselines, including Seq2Seq, GECToR, BART, and Qwen2.5-7B under zero-shot, few-shot, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) configurations. To preserve correction precision while expanding diagnostic coverage, the primary model integrates LoRA parameter-efficient fine-tuning with a multi-granularity retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) module.

Empirical benchmarks demonstrate that large language models fine-tuned on HCGEC achieve superior correction accuracy compared to traditional sequence transduction baselines. On the native HCGEC test split, the LoRA plus multi-granularity RAG approach attains an M2 precision of 53.76%, a recall of 49.14%, and an F0.5 of 52.76%. When evaluated zero-shot on the external out-of-domain MuCGEC benchmark, the framework retains an F0.5 of 47.24%, confirming minimal degradation during cross-domain deployment.
- GECToR achieves an F0.5 of 43.26% on HCGEC, trailing the fine-tuned large language model framework by 9.50 percentage points.
- Multi-granularity RAG boosts recall on HCGEC from 46.53% to 49.14% relative to standard LoRA fine-tuning.

Existing Chinese grammatical error correction (CGEC) corpora predominantly target printed text, neglecting complex handwritten modifications such as overwriting, strikethroughs, and margin insertions. This study introduces HCGEC, a multi-modal handwriting CGEC dataset containing 8,726 authentic composition samples from international learners across more than 30 countries and HSK levels 3 through 6. By incorporating a convolutional block attention module into text detection and an attention decoder into recognition, the pipeline suppresses stroke noise. Evaluated on Qwen2.5-7B with low-rank adaptation and multi-granularity retrieval-augmented generation, the model achieves a state-of-the-art M2 F0.5 of 52.76% on HCGEC.
## Corpus Scale Constraints and Operational Boundaries
While HCGEC offers granular multimodal pairings for handwritten Chinese compositions, several structural constraints limit its immediate applicability to ultra-large scale language modeling.

- The dataset scale is bounded at 8,726 validated sentence samples, which is relatively small compared to massive synthetic or web-crawled corpora, constraining pretraining capacity for web-scale models.
- Text genres are largely confined to university coursework (narrative and argumentative essays), leaving expository, technical, and practical application writing underrepresented.
- Learner proficiency is concentrated in elementary and intermediate stages (HSK 3 to HSK 5), offering fewer samples from advanced HSK 6 writers.
- Physical alteration marks (strikethroughs, overwriting scribbles) are mapped to corrected textual spans rather than independently segmented as pixel-level bounding boxes.

## 1. Executive Abstract

Current research on Chinese grammatical error correction (CGEC) primarily relies on printed text corpora and lacks dedicated benchmarks for handwritten compositions, where complex learner modifications introduce severe cascading errors into standard optical character recognition (OCR) and downstream NLP models. To bridge this gap, this paper constructs the HCGEC dataset, a fine-grained, multi-modal Chinese grammatical error correction benchmark tailored for Chinese as a second language (CSL) learners. Drawing from authentic handwritten coursework produced by learners from over 30 countries spanning HSK levels 3 through 6, the pipeline utilizes an optimized OCR architecture incorporating multi-scale attention mechanisms to suppress overwriting and revision noise. Through standardized human annotation, rigorous coordinate-level image-text alignment, and hierarchical quality validation, the dataset establishes 8,726 valid sentence samples encompassing 39,763 individual errors categorized across 599 fine-grained types. Benchmark experiments utilizing large language models demonstrate that integrating low-rank adaptation (LoRA) with multi-granularity retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) attains an M2 precision of 53.76% and an F0.5 of 52.76% on the HCGEC test set, outperforming classic sequence-to-sequence and generative baselines while demonstrating robust out-of-domain generalization on the MuCGEC benchmark.
## 2. Core Quantitative Takeaways

- Compiles 8,726 verified multimodal handwriting sentence samples with 39,763 error instances (averaging 4.6 errors per sentence) categorized into 599 fine-grained types across characters, vocabulary, and syntax.
- Partitions into 6,108 training, 1,308 testing, and 1,310 validation instances across learners from over 30 countries spanning HSK 3 to HSK 6 proficiency levels.
- Multi-scale spatial and channel attention in OCR text detection achieves an F1 score of 0.8560 and normalized edit similarity (NES) of 89.36%, suppressing strikethrough and rewriting noise.
- Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-7B with LoRA and multi-granularity RAG achieves an M2 F0.5 score of 52.76% on HCGEC and 47.24% on MuCGEC, outperforming BART and GECToR baselines.
